OUR SHIRE
Brewarrina | Goodooga | Gongolgon | Weilmoringle | Angledool
Brewarrina is a rural and remote community 
located in the north-west region of NSW on the 
banks of the Barwon River. 
The Shire has a population of 1,356 people 
(ABS 2021), and includes the towns and villages of 
Brewarrina, Goodooga, Weilmoringle, Angledool 
and Gongolgon. It borders the state line of 
Queensland and is surrounded by the local 
government areas of Walgett, Warren, Bogan 
and Bourke.
Over 51 percent of the population in the 
Brewarrina Shire are First Nations, and the 
community is strongly grounded in its First 
Nations heritage. Brewarrina is home to what is 
believed to be the oldest human construction 
on earth, the National Heritage-listed Baiame’s 
Ngunnhu (Brewarrina Fish Traps). The traps were 
one of the great inter-tribal meeting places in 
Eastern Australia for many nations of Aboriginal 
peoples, including the Morawari, Barkinji, Weilwan, 
Kamilaroi, Koamu, Valarai, Baranbinja, Wiradjuri, 
Ngemba and Yualwarri tribes. They are still used 
today and continue to have a strong social, 
cultural and spiritual association for First Nations.
The Brewarrina Shire spans 19,000 square 
kilometres, covering approximately 2.4 percent 
of the total area of NSW, and contains less than 
0.00025% of the total population, with one person 
for every 11.51 square kilometres. 
The Shire population has steadily declined over 
the past eight census counts, with close to 
500 people leaving the district since 1991. At the 
last census date, the majority of the Brewarrina 
population were under 39 years of age, with 
one quarter younger than 15 years. A greater 
proportion of these younger people are amongst 
the First Nations population.

Section 8 of Local Government Act (1993)
Brewarrina Shire Council adopted, for its Charter, Section 8

a) To provide directly or on behalf of other levels of

and conserve the environment of the area for which it

promotes the principles of ecologically sustainable 
development.

of its decisions.

the assets for which it is responsible.

of the public users of facilities and services and council 
staff in the development, improvement and coordination 
of local government. 
i) To raise funds for local purposes by the fair imposition 
of rates, charges and fees, by income earned from 
investments and, when appropriate, by borrowings and 
grants.

(and through it, the wider community) informed about 
its activities. 
k) To ensure that, in the exercise of its regulatory functions, 
it acts consistently and without bias, particularly where 
an activity of the council is affected.

and independent review of its information 
technology (IT) environment to ensure systems

assessed infrastructure, applications, governance 
and compliance, and identified several critical 
areas requiring improvement. These included 
gaps in cyber security protections, limited 
disaster recovery arrangements, reliance on 
legacy infrastructure and fragmented endpoint 
management.
With the expiry of the previous managed 
services agreement, Council initiated a 
competitive procurement process under the 
NSW Government’s ICT Services Scheme to 
ensure best value, transparency and compliance 
with the Local Government Act 1993 (NSW). This 
process confirmed the need for a new provider 
capable of delivering modernised infrastructure, 
proactive support and enhanced cyber 
resilience.
The incoming provider commenced under a 
formal Service Level Agreement (SLA), which sets 
clear standards for performance, accountability 
and reporting. The SLA includes:
• Proactive monitoring and maintenance of 
servers, networks and endpoints to reduce 
downtime and improve efficiency.
• Defined response times, with urgent and 
critical issues addressed promptly to minimise 
operational disruption.
• Structured disaster recovery planning, 
including routine backup verification and test 
restorations.
• Comprehensive cyber security services, 
progressing Council’s compliance with the 
Essential 8 strategies and incorporating 
independent penetration testing and audits.
Looking ahead, Council’s IT Roadmap for 2025–
26 and beyond sets out a staged program of 
investment and reform designed to reduce risk 
and support long-term digital transformation. 
Priorities include:
• Migration of legacy applications and 
infrastructure to cloud-first platforms, reducing 
reliance on on-premises hardware.
• Network segmentation to separate public, 
corporate and operational systems, 
addressing vulnerabilities and strengthening 
security for critical infrastructure.
• Expansion of Microsoft 365 and cloud-based 
security tools for centralised management, 
identity protection and threat detection.
• Introduction of a formal disaster recovery 
framework, supported by regular drills to 
ensure service continuity.
• Progression towards higher levels of 
compliance with the Essential 8 maturity 
model, with the goal of achieving sustainable, 
auditable security practices.
By modernising infrastructure, embedding 
structured cyber security protections and 
strengthening governance oversight, Council 
is ensuring that technology remains a reliable 
enabler of day-to-day operations and long-term 
community outcomes. These improvements 
will protect essential services, safeguard data 
and privacy, and provide a resilient platform to 
support the region’s future digital and service 
delivery needs.

The objective of the environmental services program is to provide environmentally sound planning 
and regulatory controls to meet the community needs through maximising the Communities access to 
services that improve or enhance the quality of life. Functions include:
Environmental Planning.
Environmental Planning generally covers the assessment of Development Applications (DA’s) for 
compliance with the appropriate legislative controls, Issue of Consents (usually with conditions aimed 
at ensuring minimal negative impact on the property or adjoining lands), refusal of consent and 
monitoring of the development until completed. It also involves monitoring of the currency of the Local 
Environmental Plan (LEP).
This year, Council began reviewing the Local Environmental Plan (LEP 2012) after discussions with 
consultants and the Department of Planning highlighted barriers to development and service diversity. 
The first stage focuses on simple amendments to remove current restrictions, supporting developments 
like Rural Residential projects in suitable areas. While major changes are not expected immediately, 
these adjustments aim to encourage a more diverse economy and flexible land use, responding to 
community needs and interests.
Building Certification
Building certification ensures all construction in the Shire meets legislative requirements. Council 
assesses applications, supervises construction with key inspections, and issues occupancy certificates 
upon completion. After a period without a Building Certifier, Kim Talbert has resumed the role, providing 
valuable support to applicants and property owners. His ongoing presence benefits both the community 
and the certification process.
Development Applications
The 2024/2025 financial year has not experienced a significant number of Development Applications, 
and projections suggest that this trend is unlikely to change substantially in the upcoming financial 
year. Several applications received have not been particularly well received, and the ongoing 
constraints associated with the RU5 Village zone continue to complicate the evaluation of new 
commercial or industrial development proposals. This zoning often leads to confusion among 
applicants, as many believe the RU5 designation allows unrestricted development on properties they 
have acquired.
Throughout the 2025/26 financial year, it is important to advise all identified potential developers to 
engage in preliminary discussions with Council staff prior to making any commitments to acquire land 
within the shire or towns, or before progressing with detailed plans for proposed projects. Such early 
engagement will help clarify requirements and reduce misunderstandings regarding permitted uses 
and development controls.

providing clearer guidance for future developments.

the community, serving as potential fire hazards 
and attracting rodents or snakes. Such conditions 
can subsequently pose health risks to neighbours 
and the wider community.

a portion of the costs incurred. However, should

covered by the PIN, Council may be required to 
pursue costly legal action to recover these funds,

§Subnote§
Material accounting policy information
Grant and contribution revenue from an agreement which is enforceable and contains sufficiently specific performance
obligations is recognised as or when control of each performance obligations is transferred.
The performance obligations vary according to the agreement. Payment terms vary depending on the terms of the grant, cash
is received upfront for some grants and on the achievement of certain payment milestones for others.
Performance obligations may be satisfied either at a point in time or over time and this is reflected in the revenue recognition
pattern. Point in time recognition occurs when the beneficiary obtains control of the goods / services at a single time (e.g.
completion of the project when a report / outcome is provided), whereas over time recognition is where the control of the
services is ongoing throughout the project (e.g. provision of community health services through the year).
Where control is transferred over time, generally the input methods being either costs or time incurred are deemed to be the
most appropriate methods to reflect the transfer of benefit.
Capital grants
Capital grants received by Council under an enforceable contract for the acquisition or construction of infrastructure, property,
plant and equipment to identified specifications which will be under Council’s control on completion are recognised as revenue
as and when the obligation to construct or purchase is completed.
For construction projects, this is generally as the construction progresses in accordance with costs incurred since this is
deemed to be the most appropriate measure of the completeness of the construction project.
For acquisitions of assets, the revenue is recognised when the asset is acquired and controlled by the Council.
Other grants and contributions
Assets, including cash, received from other grants and contributions are recognised at fair value when the asset is received.
Council considers whether there are any related liability or equity items associated with the asset which are recognised in
accordance with the relevant accounting standard.
Once the assets and liabilities have been recognised then income is recognised for any remaining asset value at the time
that the asset is received.

Material accounting policy information
Receivables are recognised initially at fair value and subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest 
method, less provision for impairment. Receivables are generally due for settlement within 30 days.
Impairment of financial assets measured at amortised cost is recognised on an expected credit loss (ECL) basis.
Impairment
When determining whether the credit risk of a financial asset has increased significantly since initial recognition, and when
estimating ECL, the Council considers reasonable and supportable information that is relevant and available without undue
cost or effort. This includes both quantitative and qualitative information and analysis based on Council’s historical experience
and informed credit assessment, and including forward-looking information.
When considering the ECL for rates debtors, Council takes into account that unpaid rates represent a charge against the
rateable property that will be recovered when the property is next sold. For non-rates debtors, Council uses the presumption
that an asset which is more than 30 days past due has seen a significant increase in credit risk.
The Council uses the presentation that a financial asset is in default when:
• the other party is unlikely to pay its credit obligations to the Council in full, without recourse by the Council to actions
such as realising security (if any is held) or
• the financial assets (for non-rates debtors) are more than 90 days past due.
Credit losses are measured as the present value of the difference between the cash flows due to the entity in accordance with
the contract, and the cash flows expected to be received. This is applied using a probability weighted approach.
On initial recognition of the asset, an estimate of the expected credit losses for the next 12 months is recognised. Where the
asset has experienced significant increase in credit risk then the lifetime losses are estimated and recognised.
Council uses the simplified approach for trade receivables where the expected lifetime credit losses are recognised on day 1.
There has been no change in the estimation techniques or significant assumptions made during the current reporting period.
The Council writes off a trade receivable when there is information indicating that the debtor is in severe financial difficulty
and there is no realistic prospect of recovery, e.g. when the debtor has been placed under liquidation or has entered into
bankruptcy proceedings, or when the receivables are over 5 years past due, whichever occurs first.
None of the receivables that have been written off are subject to enforcement activity.
Where the Council renegotiates the terms of receivables due from certain customers, the new expected cash flows are
discounted at the original effective interest rate and any resulting difference to the carrying value is recognised in profit or loss.
Rates and annual charges outstanding are secured against the property.

All Other Level 2 and 3 Asset Classes
Where there was an active and liquid market as evidenced by sales transactions of similar property types, a Market
Approach by way of Direct Comparison, Income Capitalisation or Summation methods was utilised.
These are accepted valuation methodologies under AASB 13. If a Market Approach is adopted, the building valuation is
deemed to be a Level 2 input.
Direct comparison and summation methods involve analysis of sales evidence and comparisons with the subject taking into
account matters such as method of construction, size, condition, age, land area and location. The land value is subtracted
from the Market Value of the property to measure the building asset Fair Value.
For those assets not assessed under a Market Approach due to their predominantly specialised nature, a Current
Replacement Cost (CRC) approach to valuation has been adopted, being an accepted valuation methodology under AASB
13. The CRC approach is deemed Level 3 methodology on the Fair Value Hierarchy.
Where there is no depth of market, as determined for the specified Brewarrina Shire Council assets, the net current value of
an asset is the gross current value less accumulated depreciation to reflect the consumed or expired service potential of the
asset.
Under this approach, the following process is adopted:
• Published/available market data for recent projects, and/or published cost guides are utilised to determine the estimated
replacement cost (gross value) of the asset, including allowances for preliminaries and professional fees. This is
considered a Level 2 input.
• A condition assessment is applied, which is based on factors such as the age of the asset, overall condition as noted by
the Valuer during inspection, economic and/or functional obsolescence. The condition assessment directly translates
to the level of depreciation applied. The conditions assessed are considered a Level 3 input.
• While the replacement cost of the assets could be supported by market supplied evidence (level 2), other unobservable
inputs (such as estimates of residual value, useful life, asset condition) were also required (level 3).
To calculate the appropriate amount of accumulated depreciation, assets were either subject to a site inspection or an
assessment to determine remaining useful life. Where site inspections were conducted (i.e. for visible aboveground assets),
the assets were allocated a condition assessment, which was used to estimate remaining useful life.
